verdicts.text: Pulumi packages come in two flavors, and each is versioned and released differently. Understanding the release artifact for each flavor is the foundation for the repository-layout advice in this guide.
verdicts.evidence: This is the intro sentence for the "How Pulumi packages are versioned" section. It describes how the guide itself is organized, which is the author's own framing. The factual details come in the subsections that follow, starting with "Source-based packages" at L17 (source-based packages are versioned by their Git tag). The regex probably matched on "versioned and released", but the sentence makes no claim about time, a release date, or a version.

verdicts.text: The link anchors #source-based-plugin-packages and #executable-based-plugin-packages exist on the packaging-components page; the private-registry and pulumi_package_publish pages exist.
verdicts.evidence: packaging-components.md has the headings "## Source-based plugin packages" (L44) and "## Executable-based plugin packages" (L73), so both anchors resolve. content/docs/idp/concepts/private-registry.md exists (title "Private Registry"), and so does content/docs/iac/cli/commands/pulumi_package_publish.md (auto-generated, "Publish a package to the Private Registry").

verdicts.text: Publishing a source-based package to the Pulumi IDP Private Registry is a two-step flow (apply a semver Git tag, then run pulumi package publish), typically performed by a CI/CD pipeline that runs on tag.
verdicts.evidence: The cited anchor only says "Pulumi Cloud customers can publish versions of the package to the Pulumi IDP Private Registry using `pulumi package publish`". It says nothing about a Git tag step. A sibling guide shows the two steps together in "A typical CI/CD pipeline": `git tag v1.0.0` / `git push origin v1.0.0` / `pulumi package publish github.com/myorg/my-component@1.0.0`.
verdicts.framing_note: The cited anchor backs only the `pulumi package publish` step. The tag-then-publish order and the CI context come from the sibling source-based-plugin.md, and that sibling marks the publish step "(optional)" inside a larger pipeline that also pre-publishes SDKs.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Runs on tag" and the claim that semver tags are required were not checked against the `pulumi package publish` CLI source, because the gh search hit a rate limit.

verdicts.text: `pulumi package publish` sends the package metadata to Pulumi Cloud and places the package in the Private Registry.
verdicts.evidence: The auto-generated CLI reference says: "This command publishes a package to the Private Registry. The package can be a provider or a schema." It also says the command extracts or reads the package schema and takes a readme. That supports describing it as sending package metadata to Pulumi Cloud, where the Private Registry lives.
verdicts.framing_note: source: 'Publish a package to the Private Registry' (schema + readme) vs claim: 'sends the package metadata to Pulumi Cloud and places the package in the Private Registry'

verdicts.text: Publishing to the Private Registry requires applying a semver Git tag (e.g., v1.2.3) to the repository.
verdicts.evidence: The Private Registry concept doc agrees: "Pulumi uses git tags for versioning components... The tag must adhere to the semantic versioning standard plus a "v" prefix (e.g. `v1.2.3`)." Its troubleshooting table also lists `error: no version tag found` with the fix "Tag your repository with a semver tag". I couldn't confirm this in product source because the gh search hit a rate limit, so this rests on another Pulumi docs page.
verdicts.framing_note: The claim only covers source-based packages (the paragraph at L17-24). Executable-based packages are versioned from the binary/SDK instead, so the tag requirement shouldn't be read as applying to every package type.

verdicts.text: Semver-tagged releases are only required for publishing to the Private Registry; source-based packages referenced directly from a Pulumi.yaml file can use any Git ref (tag, branch, or commit), regardless of whether it is a valid semantic version.
verdicts.evidence: The auto-generated `pulumi package add` CLI reference, which is transcribed from pulumi/pulumi source, says a Git-repo version "can either be a tag (in semver format), or a Git commit hash. By default the latest tag (by semver version), or if not available the latest commit on the default branch is used." That contradicts the claim that any ref works, including branches and non-semver tags.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Regardless of whether it is a valid semantic version" and "branch" don't match what the CLI help documents. I couldn't check the resolver code directly because the gh API was rate-limited.

verdicts.text: Source-based packages referenced directly from a Pulumi.yaml file can use any Git ref (tag, branch, or commit), regardless of whether it is a valid semantic version.
verdicts.evidence: The PR that added git-source plugins (pulumi/pulumi#17827) shows only two supported forms: `pulumi package add github.com/example/bla@deadbeef` (a commit) and `@v1.1.0`. It also notes "there is the expectation that there will be a semver based tag prefixed with `v` in the repository here". I found nothing showing that branch names or non-semver tags work, so the "any Git ref (tag, branch, or commit)" wording isn't confirmed.
verdicts.intuition_flag: Commit hashes and semver tags are confirmed, but branch names and non-semver tags may not resolve as plugin versions. Check the version parsing in the git plugin source (sdk/go/common/workspace) before publishing "any Git ref".

verdicts.text: Executable-based package releases are produced by a CI/CD pipeline that builds the plugin, generates the SDKs, and pushes everything to the relevant feeds.
verdicts.evidence: This is general guidance about the usual release flow, not a hard product rule. It matches Pulumi's own provider boilerplate: its `.github/workflows/release.yml` defines a `publish_java_sdk` job and a "Publish Go SDK" step (`uses: pulumi/publish-go-sdk-action@v1`) alongside the provider build. I only saw search-result snippets, not the full workflow file.
verdicts.source: gh search code --repo pulumi/pulumi-provider-boilerplate publish --filename release.yml
verdicts.framing_note: Describes the typical pattern ("typically" is implied by context), not a mandatory mechanism.

verdicts.text: Pulumi Cloud customers can additionally publish an executable-based package to the Private Registry via `pulumi package publish`.
verdicts.evidence: The auto-generated CLI reference says `pulumi package publish` "publishes a package to the Private Registry. The package can be a provider or a schema," and "When <provider> is specified as a local path, Pulumi executes the provider binary to extract its package schema." That means an executable provider binary can be published to the Private Registry with this command.

verdicts.text: An executable-based plugin package is distributed as a pre-built plugin binary, typically alongside per-language SDKs published to package feeds (npm, PyPI, NuGet, Maven, the Go module proxy, or private equivalents).
verdicts.evidence: The linked anchor section says: "Executable-based plugin packages are usually distributed as pre-built per-language SDKs published to multiple package managers (one per consumer language), with the plugin executable published to an accessible location." The claim's summary ("pre-built plugin binary, typically alongside per-language SDKs") matches this. The specific list of feeds is broader than the page's examples ("npmjs.org, PyPI, etc."), but that is a reasonable expansion.
verdicts.framing_note: Source: "usually distributed as pre-built per-language SDKs ... with the plugin executable published to an accessible location"; the claim says the same thing with "typically".

verdicts.text: In both source-based and executable-based cases, the released artifact is a single, semantically-versioned Pulumi package.
verdicts.evidence: This line sums up the page's own L17–28, and I couldn't check it against product source because GitHub code search hit its rate limit (HTTP 429). The page also qualifies itself at L24: "Semver-tagged releases are only required for publishing to the Private Registry. Source-based packages referenced directly from a `Pulumi.yaml` file can use any Git ref". So for source-based packages, "semantically-versioned" only holds when the package is published to the registry.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The blanket claim that the artifact is "semantically-versioned" in both cases conflicts with L24, which says source-based packages can be consumed from any Git ref that isn't semver. Consider changing it to "a released (published) artifact".

verdicts.text: A 1:1 repository-to-package mapping keeps git tags, release artifacts, and version history aligned.
verdicts.evidence: This line is part of Pulumi's own best-practice advice ("A repository should contain exactly one Pulumi package… A 1:1 repository-to-package mapping keeps git tags, release artifacts, and version history aligned."). It gives the reasoning behind a design recommendation. It doesn't describe any product behavior that could be tested as true or false.

verdicts.text: Multiple components inside a single Pulumi package are fine and expected, and ship together at the package's version.
verdicts.evidence: This holds because of how packages are built. A Pulumi package schema has one top-level `version` and a `resources` map that can hold many component resources. packaging-components.md also describes packages as carrying multiple "components" that are released and versioned as one unit, alongside custom resources and functions. So components in the same package ship at that package's single version.
verdicts.source: repo:content/docs/iac/guides/building-extending/components/packaging-components.md (L19-23, L62, L87); Pulumi package schema structure (single version, resources map)
verdicts.framing_note: Only the versioning part ("ship together at the package's version") can be checked. "Fine and expected" is the guide's own recommendation, not a statement of fact.

verdicts.intuition_flag: The claim looks plausible (pulumi-eks ships Cluster, NodeGroup, ManagedNodeGroup and VpcCniAddon), but the pulumi/pulumi-eks schema should be checked to confirm it.

verdicts.text: A single PulumiPlugin.yaml at the repository root defines the package, with components living alongside it.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass3) The source-based plugin guide shows the same layout, with `PulumiPlugin.yaml` at the plugin root next to the component code. It also says "A single plugin package can expose **multiple components**" and "Pulumi reads `PulumiPlugin.yaml`, introspects the plugin... Every component in the package is available under the generated SDK."
verdicts.framing_note: The claim describes an example layout the guide recommends. Only other Pulumi docs pages back it up; I did not check the product source because GitHub search hit a rate limit.

verdicts.text: The example repository layout places one PulumiPlugin.yaml at the root and components under a components/ directory.
verdicts.evidence: This describes the page's own example tree, and the description is accurate. L58-65 show `eks-platform/` with `├── PulumiPlugin.yaml` and `├── components/` holding `EksCluster/` and `EksIam/`. It's an example the author made up, so there's nothing about the product to check.

verdicts.text: When unrelated components share a package, every release of the package versions every component the same way, regardless of whether each component changed, which violates semver.
verdicts.evidence: The mechanics hold: in Pulumi a package has one version (a Git tag for source-based packages, the binary/SDK version for executable-based ones), and components have no version of their own. The file's L11 also says components "inherit the package's version". I didn't read the schema file directly. The GitHub code search was rate-limited (HTTP 429), so this rests on well-known package-schema structure. "Violates semver" is the author's advisory judgment, not a product behavior.
verdicts.source: gh api repos/pulumi/pulumi/contents/pkg/codegen/schema/pulumi.json (located only, not read); repo:content/docs/iac/guides/building-extending/packages/repository-strategy.md L11-L30 (context only)
verdicts.intuition_flag: Strictly speaking, bundling components doesn't "violate semver". SemVer versions the package's public API as a whole, so a minor or major bump driven by one component is still valid semver. Wording like "undermines the per-component signal semver provides" would be more accurate.

verdicts.text: In the example, releasing ComponentA's enhancement bumps the package to v1.1.0 and a breaking change to ComponentB bumps it to v2.0.0, illustrating semver-consistent bumps.
verdicts.evidence: The SemVer spec says a backward-compatible feature bumps the minor version, and "Major version X ... MUST be incremented if any backward incompatible changes are introduced," with minor and patch reset to 0. So going from v1.0.0 to v1.1.0 for an enhancement, then to v2.0.0 for a breaking change, follows SemVer. I didn't read the doc's example numbers directly, so I'm taking them from the claim text.
verdicts.framing_note: The SemVer increment rules in general cover the specific v1.1.0 and v2.0.0 bumps in the example.
